newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich faces reprimand, $300,000 ethics penalty.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich faces reprimand, $300,000 ethics penalty.

text.p: The House ethics committee on Friday considered a $300,000 penalty and a reprimand as punishments for Speaker Newt Gingrich's admitted ethics violations. Gingrich agreed in advance to the financial levy.

As the committee opened a public hearing into the proposed penalties on Friday afternoon, an ethics subcommittee provided it with the special investigative counsel's final report on the Gingrich case detailing penalties.
"Mr. Gingrich has agreed that this (a $300,000 penalty) is the apporporiate sanction in this matter," special counsel James Cole said in the report.

"The penalty recommendation the committee will consider is tough and unprecedented compared to past cases," Chairwoman Nancy Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, said as the panel began its televised hearing on punishments.
"The committee decision will be guided by its belief that the speaker of the House must be held to the highest ethical standards," Johnson said.

If the full House of Representatives approves the recommendations in a vote set for Tuesday, Gingrich would be the only incumbent House speaker in U.S. history to be reprimanded, let alone to be hit with financial penalties.

The report also indicated the ethics subcommittee -- which endorsed and transmitted Cole's report to the full panel -- felt Gingrich's violations strained the limits of what could be covered by a reprimand rather than the more severe penalty of censure. A censure might have forced Gingrich to step down as speaker.
"It is the opinion of the subcommittee that this matter fell somewhere in between" reprimand and censure, it said.

Gingrich acknowledged on on Dec. 21 that he had provided to investigators "in my name and over my signature, inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable statements." He said he had not intended to mislead the committee.

He also acknowledged he had failed to seek legal advice on whether his use of tax-exempt charitable funds for a college course he taught would violate tax laws. The subcommittee that investigated the ethics charges did not then take a position on whether the law had been broken.
In one of many scathing characterisations of Gingrich's behaviour, the report said:

"The violation does not represent only a single instance of reckless conduct. Rather, over a number of years and in a number of situations, Mr. Gingrich showed a disregard and lack of respect for the standards of conduct that applied to his activities."
It said Gingrich's conduct in the cited transgressions "was intentional or it was reckless."
The ethics commimttee would transmit its decision on the proposals to the full House.

Although the financial penalties may have come as a surprise to some -- most speculation had centred only on a possible reprimand -- Gingrich at least avoided another blow that had been rumoured earlier Friday.

There was no recommendation to refer the information gathered in the inquiry to the Internal Revenue Service or Justice Department for further action, as reported by some news organisations. That would have dragged the controversy out indefinitely.

As the committee neared its climactic vote, Gingrich enjoyed an enthusiastic welcome as he made an inspirational speech to the Republican National Committee in which he made only one oblique mention of his ethics troubles."
"I don't worry too much about each day's headlines," he said. He declined to answer reporters' questions.
The report issued on Friday is the product of a year-long investigation by Cole. Cole and Gingrich's lawyer were to address the committee during the public hearing.
